title: Goal-Based Investing
blurb: Planning by goal, not by product: sizes, horizons and SIPs for real life goals.

rows: New employees (all sections), sales team (talk-tracks, role-plays, niche topics); investors as awareness material
About 77 minutes of lessons, plus role-play and the final quiz
Each L.E.A.R.N. stage has: what to know, how to do it, a talk-track, and the investor takeaway

sources: SEBI Master Circular for Mutual Funds (current edition)

lessons.title: What a goal is: four answers, three horizons, five steps
The maths of a goal: inflate the cost, then find the SIP
Worked examples: starting early, stepping up, and retirement
Matching the asset mix to the horizon
Mapping funds to goals, and step-up SIPs
The glide path: de-risk as the goal approaches
When a goal is off track: four levers
Goals as an anchor: behaviours to watch
Compliance: dos, don'ts and the final check

a: Start with the goal, not the fund. Goal → time frame → asset mix → funds.
Four answers: what it's for, how much (today's cost), when, and how important.
Discover → Quantify → Prioritise → Plan → Review yearly.
Under 3 years. Main risk: losing capital just before it's needed. Use debt.
3–7 years. Main risk: a market fall close to the goal date. Use a balanced mix.
7+ years. Main risk: inflation and not taking enough growth. Mostly equity.
Today's cost × (1 + inflation) ^ years.
₹20 lakh today at 8% for 15 years ≈ ₹63.4 lakh.
About ₹13,300 a month at an assumed 12% for 15 years.
Same target with 10 years left: about ₹28,300 a month, more than double.
Raise the SIP yearly with income. A 10% step-up cut the starting SIP to about ₹7,700.
₹50,000 a month today ≈ ₹2.15 lakh a month in 25 years at 6% inflation.
Emergency fund (about 6 months) → insurance → clear high-cost debt → goals.
Must-have (retirement, education), should-have (house, car), nice-to-have (holiday).
<1 yr: all debt · 1–3: mostly debt · 3–5: 20–40% equity · 5–7: about half · 7+: 60–80%+ equity.
Move gradually from equity to debt as the goal approaches, often by STP; check tax and exit loads.
Find every goal across horizons.
Example: "What are you saving for in the next 3 years? 3–10? Beyond?"
Remember: Involve the family.
Separate must-haves from wants.
Example: "If you could achieve only three, which would they be?"
Remember: Fund must-haves first.
Parents often put education above their own retirement.
Example: Child's MBA vs retiring at 60
Remember: Education can be part-funded by a loan; retirement can't.
Different costs rise at different rates.
Example: Education, healthcare often faster
Remember: One rate for all goals underestimates the costly ones.
Each goal gets its own SIP and label.
Example: Folio tag "Riya college"
Remember: Label the units, don't multiply the funds.
Park a lump sum in a liquid fund and move it in stages.
Example: Bonus for a 10-year goal
Remember: Eases timing worries.
Progress, target, mix, glide path, contributions.
Example: Is the value where the plan expected?
Remember: Yearly and on life events, not on headlines.
Raise the SIP or add a lump sum.
Example: Bonus, policy maturity
Remember: First lever when off track.
Give the goal more time.
Example: Retire two years later
Remember: Flexible for should-haves.
Reduce the goal's cost.
Example: A less expensive college option
Remember: Discuss honestly with the family.
Taking more risk to catch up.
Example: Moving a near goal into small caps
Remember: Off-track is fixed by levers, not gambling.
Labelled money is less likely to be spent or panic-sold.
Example: "Riya's college" folio
Remember: Name the folios.
Delaying the start.
Example: "I'll begin next year"
Remember: Show the cost of delay in rupees.
Assuming high returns to make the SIP look small.
Example: Planning at 18% a year
Remember: Use conservative, labelled assumptions.
Count what's already earmarked.
Example: EPF, PPF, NPS, FDs, gold
Remember: Reduces the new SIP needed.
Accumulation, then drawing income.
Example: SWP after retirement
Remember: Plan the income phase too, not just the corpus.

questions.q: A goal needs:
o: An amount, a date and a priority
questions.why: An amount, a date and a priority. Plus what it's for.

questions.q: ₹20 lakh today at 8% inflation for 15 years becomes about:
Money needed in under a year should usually be in:
questions.why: Liquid or overnight funds. No room for a market fall.

questions.q: What comes before investing for goals?
questions.why: Emergency fund and insurance. Foundation first.

questions.q: In the illustration, a 5-year delay changed the SIP from about ₹13,300 to about:
questions.why: ₹28,300. A late start more than doubles it.

questions.q: A step-up SIP means:
o: Raising the SIP regularly with income
questions.why: Raising the SIP regularly with income. Makes big goals affordable today.

questions.q: As a goal approaches, the equity share should usually:
questions.why: Fall gradually. The glide path.

questions.q: Which is NOT a lever when a goal is off track?
questions.why: Chase the highest-returning fund. Never chase returns to catch up.

questions.q: Which goal is often underfunded because it feels far away?
questions.why: Retirement. Largest goal; hurt most by a late start.

questions.q: Labelling folios by goal mainly helps because:
o: It reduces the urge to spend goal money and clarifies reviews
questions.why: It reduces the urge to spend goal money and clarifies reviews. Mental accounting used well.

questions.q: The right order is:
o: Goal → time frame → asset mix → funds
questions.why: Goal → time frame → asset mix → funds. Start with the goal.

questions.q: A typical emergency fund is about:
questions.why: 6 months of expenses. In savings or a liquid fund.

questions.q: For a goal 7+ years away, the illustrative equity share is:
questions.why: 60–80% or more. Adjusted to the client's risk profile.

questions.q: ₹50,000 monthly expenses today become about how much in 25 years at 6% inflation?
When should goals normally be reviewed?
questions.why: Yearly and on life events. Not on headlines.

questions.q: Why should money needed soon not be in equity?
o: Equity is banned for short goals
A market fall just before the goal date could shrink the money needed
Equity funds don't accept short holding periods
Debt always returns more than equity
questions.why: Debt for short-term goals.

questions.q: Why use a goal-specific inflation rate for education?
o: SEBI requires one rate per goal
Education costs often rise faster than general inflation
questions.why: Use goal-specific inflation.

questions.q: A client says a plan made 3 years ago never needs review. Why is that wrong?
o: Goals, costs and markets change; review yearly and on life events
questions.why: Review yearly and on life events.

questions.q: Why are parents often advised to prioritise retirement over education funding?
o: Education can be part-funded by a loan; retirement cannot
questions.why: Prioritise retirement accordingly.

questions.q: Markets fell 15%. A client's education goal is 11 years away. Should the plan change?
o: No — review yearly, not on headlines; the plan already expects falls
questions.why: Review yearly, not on headlines.

questions.q: A client says, “Just tell me the best fund.” How do you respond?
o: Redirect to goals: what for, how much, when, priority; explain that the goal decides the mix and the fund
Ask for their risk profile only
questions.why: Redirects to goals: what for, how much, when, priority; explains that the goal decides the mix and the fund.

questions.q: A couple wants to fund their son’s MBA in 12 years and retire in 20. How do you plan?
o: Quantify both with inflation; prioritise; discuss the education-loan vs retirement trade-off; separate mixes and SIPs
Fund the MBA first and ignore retirement
Use the same mix for both
questions.why: Quantifies both with inflation; prioritises; discusses education loan vs retirement; separate mixes and SIPs.

questions.q: A client wants ₹10 lakh for a car in 2 years in small-cap funds “for better returns”. What do you say?
o: Explain short-horizon risk; recommend debt (short duration / target maturity); no equity for near goals
Say 2 years is long enough for equity
questions.why: Explains short-horizon risk; recommends debt (short duration / target maturity); no equity for near goals.

questions.q: A client’s retirement goal is 30% behind plan. What do you do?
o: Chase the highest-returning fund to catch up
Use the four levers: invest more, extend the date, adjust the target, review the mix; never chase returns
questions.why: Uses the four levers: invest more, extend the date, adjust the target, review the mix; never chases returns.

questions.q: Markets fell 15%. A client wants to stop the education SIP for a goal 11 years away. How do you respond?
o: Use the goal’s time frame: SIPs buy more units in falls; the plan already expects falls; stay on track
Move the SIP to a sectoral fund
questions.why: Uses the goal's time frame; SIP buys more units in falls; the plan already expects falls; stays on track.
